current.title: The Rubik's Cube Record Dropped From 22 To 3 Seconds
current.hook: Cube champions chased this record for decades. A machine just humiliated all of them.
current.closing: Humans spent decades getting fast. A machine beat all of it in under half a second.
current.question: Could you solve a cube that fast?

segments.say: In 1982, the first world championship solve took almost 23 seconds. That number became the one everybody spent decades chasing.
By 2018 the record hit 3.47 seconds, over six times faster than 1982. Human hands kept getting quicker for decades.
Then a robot solved the same cube in 0.38 seconds. That is about eight times faster than the best human.

judge.one_line: The cube-solving scenes are nicely made, but the on-screen record (3.13s, 2023) contradicts the narration (3.47s, 2018), the robot reveal comes before the human record, and Data only waves beside machines that do the work.
problems: seg3: the screen says '3.13 sec · 2023' while the narration says '3.47' and '2018'. A viewer sees two different records.
seg2/seg3 order: the robot's 0.38s ('8x faster') is revealed before the human 2018 record, so the story peaks too early and then goes backwards.
seg0 to seg1: the cube solves itself while Data waves or points at its corner. He is not the cause of the solve.
seg3: a robot rig is used for the human-record beat, and the number never changes on screen.
seg4:start to the end: about 4s of an identical closing frame with Data frozen in a cheer pose.
seg2: '8x faster' is only a label. Nothing shows the eightfold gap between the human and robot times.
fixes: Make seg3's number 3.47 and its year 2018 to match the narration, or change the narration to the source's 3.13/2023. One number, said and shown.
Order the beats 1982 (23s), then 2018 (3.47s), then robot (0.38s), so the machine is the final reveal.
Have Data hold and solve the cube himself in seg0 and seg1, with his hands turning the faces as the stopwatch runs.
In the human-record beat, put the old 23s on the same stopwatch dial as a ghost tick and stop the hand at 3.47 to show the drop.
In the robot beat, run the human time and the robot time side by side on twin dials and let the robot's dial stop at 0.38 while the human's is still sweeping. That makes '8x' visible.
Give the closing a resolving action, such as Data slamming the stopwatch while the robot tosses a solved cube, instead of a 4s frozen cheer.

rules: TITLE or HOOK must contain a consequential NUMBER from the data below (the gate refuses a title+hook with no digit in either).

TITLE must be a PREMISE, not a searchable noun phrase: more than five words, or a number, or a question mark, or a tension word. 'Oldest Written Languages' is the failure; 'Why 3 of the 5 Oldest Scripts Are Still Unreadable' is the shape.

Every segment's TOPIC (a 2-4 word on-screen label) must share at least one real word with the TITLE — the gate checks a keyword bridge from each segment to the headline. Rename the topic, or write the title so it names what the segments are about.

Every NUMBER you say in a segment's SAY must be one that segment's data can show: a listed value, a difference between two of them, a percent change, a share of the total, or the same value in a bigger unit. A number from nowhere is refused — a guard derives every spoken quantity from the listed points.
Keep every number that is already correct. Do not add a country, company or person the data does not name.

PACE: each SAY is at most two short spoken sentences and 24 words: the beat's number, then what it MEANS (why it is surprising, what it caused, why the viewer should care), nothing else; the HOOK at most 14 words, the CLOSING at most 18 words and it says why this matters to the viewer, the QUESTION at most 8. A beat is on screen about 8 seconds; a longer line is refused. Each SAY says its beat's headline number out loud.

Each beat is part of a STORY, not a readout, simple enough for a distracted viewer: at most ONE number a beat, said with what it means (a change in words: 'it nearly doubled'). Name no group a viewer would not know ('the experts', not 'the OECD'); the WHO, NASA and the White House are fine.
TOPIC labels are printed on the video: at most 4 words, no clause.

The HOOK is clickbait, never a scam: the most surprising TRUE fact in the story, 5-14 words, said the way a person tells a friend. It makes sense heard once. 'You' only when it is the viewer's own money, body or kids. No formula tags ('...and nobody told you', '...shocking everyone'), no quiz ('Which animal...', 'Did you know...'), no hedge (might, may), no vague size ('astonishing'). Exaggerate nothing.
